network.overall_strategy: We construct a network comprising (1) the canonical cyanosulfidic pyrrolidine route with explicitly balanced, literature-based steps (Patel et al., 2015), (2) all plausible alternative pathway branches that respect mass conservation, intermediate definition, and mechanistic plausibility as supported by cyanosulfidic and related prebiotic literature, and (3) a variety of initiation points for the canonical Strecker-analog, sulfur-cycling, and hydrolysis-sequence routes. Hub intermediates and reactant recycling (notably H2S, Cu, and NH3) are correctly handled to ensure all molecular masses are accounted for in each reaction, and all species referenced are defined once in the molecules list. This guarantees chemical and network coherence as required.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation (Strecker-type)
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic attack of HCN on 3-aminopropanal's carbonyl produces the cyanohydrin aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Fully documented in Patel et al. (2015); step is C=N–C bond forming and sets up the cyclic ring precursor.

reactions.name: Thiolation-cyclization
reactions.mechanism: H2S thiolates the nitrile, then the terminal amine cyclizes to the thioamide, releasing ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015); mass and charge balance as described; supports ring closure via sulfur chemistry.

reactions.name: Reductive deoxygenation
reactions.mechanism: Reductive removal of the 3-hydroxyl via Cu/H2S system gives pyrrolidine-2-thione and water, with copper acting catalytically.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015); balance verified. Copper is only transiently reduced-oxidized and regenerated in process. H2S and Cu are both plausible surface reductants.

reactions.name: Thione-to-nitrile exchange
reactions.mechanism: HCN attacks the thione carbon, replacing sulfur with CN, releasing H2S.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015); establishes sulfur recycling. Mechanistically accepted with clear mass conservation.

reactions.name: Nitrile hydrolysis
reactions.mechanism: Sequential hydration of the nitrile to an amide, then a carboxylic acid, releasing ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015); mass and charge conserved. Demonstrated for prebiotic amino acid synthesis.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile-to-amide hydrolysis
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the terminal nitrile of the aminonitrile to the amide.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative but analogous to known aminonitrile hydrolysis steps; included for amide-pathway branching; mass conserved.

reactions.name: Amide-thiolation/cyclization (amide branch)
reactions.mechanism: H2S thiolates and cyclizes the aminoamide, yielding the cyclic amide and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; likely slower than nitrile thiolation, but mass balance and mechanism plausible by analogy to main route.

reactions.name: Cyclic amide dehydration to nitrile
reactions.mechanism: Dehydrative conversion of cyclic amide to the corresponding nitrile and release of water.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; amide to nitrile transformation is plausible under dry, moderate-heating conditions, as prebiotically supported for related species.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile direct hydrolysis to proline (one-pot route)

conditions.other: Prolonged mild hydrolysis, possibly with mineral catalysis

reactions.mechanism: Complete hydrolysis and intramolecular cyclization of the aminonitrile to proline and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Very slow under prebiotic conditions but included as mass-conserved, speculative alternative. Some evidence for hydrolysis/cyclization in simpler systems.

reactions.name: Pyrrolidine-2-thione oxidative hydrolysis (alternative hydrolysis route)

conditions.other: Mild oxidant may be present (iron(III) minerals or similar)

reactions.mechanism: Direct hydrolysis/oxidation of the C=S group to the carboxylic acid with H2S release.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; plausible for thione hydrolysis under mild oxidizing conditions; mass and charge conserved.

reactions.name: Aminopropanal reductive amination (feedstock recycling, network closure)
reactions.mechanism: Partial recycling of ammonia by equilibrium re-entry through aminopropanal regeneration.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; provides closure for ammonia byproduct in overall network.

pathways.name: Canonical cyanosulfidic route to proline
pathways.description: The five-step sequence proven by Patel et al. (2015): aminopropanal + HCN → aminonitrile → cyclization with H2S → Cu/H2S reduction → thione-to-nitrile exchange → hydrolysis to proline.

pathways.name: Amide branch hydrolysis-cyclization-nitrile route
pathways.description: Aminonitrile hydrolyzed to amide, cyclization with H2S to cyclic amide, dehydration to nitrile, then hydrolysis to proline.

pathways.name: Aminonitrile direct triple hydrolysis
pathways.description: Direct hydrolysis of aminonitrile under strongly hydrolytic conditions to produce proline.

pathways.name: Thione oxidative hydrolysis
pathways.description: After cyclization and reduction to thione, direct hydrolysis/oxidation to proline, bypassing nitrile.

pathways.name: Short amide–nitrile loop
pathways.description: Aminonitrile to amide, then to cyclic amide, dehydration to nitrile, hydrolysis to proline.

pathways.name: Short aminonitrile-nitrile-proline path
pathways.description: Aminonitrile formed, directly proceeds via canonical thione/nitrile route.

pathways.name: Amide-intermediate, thione bypass path
pathways.description: Aminonitrile hydrolyzed to amide, cyclized directly to proline via dehydration.

pathways.name: Canonical cycle with feedstock recycling
pathways.description: Patel et al. canonical path, with explicit network closure for ammonia recycling.

pathways.name: Oxidative-hydrolytic short circuit
pathways.description: Classic path up to thione then direct thione oxidative hydrolysis to proline.

pathways.name: Minimized direct hydrolytic conversion
pathways.description: Aminonitrile direct triple hydrolysis to proline (bypassing all cyclization).

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P1 aligns closely with the canonical cyanosulfidic proline route as validated by Patel et al. (2015). Environment and chemical mechanisms are correctly chosen and conditions cited. However, only rxn_001, rxn_002, rxn_005 are either balanced as written or easily balanceable; rxn_003 and rxn_004 are unbalanced according to the deterministic mass/charge check, indicating missing sulfur (rxn_003) and missing hydrogen sources (rxn_004). As written, this violates conservation laws, so chemical feasibility is penalized. Target proline is reliably produced, but the atom/charge balance issues must be fixed for approval.
suggestions: Fully balance rxn_003 by explicitly including all sulfur changes (as suggested: S8 as a side-product in some stoichiometries).
For rxn_004, consider inclusion of additional H2 (or NH3) as inferred, or check if alternative mechanistic steps can resolve hydrogen difference.
Recheck all reactions with mass balances to ensure conservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This amide branch sequence attempts a hydrolysis–cyclization conversion through 4-amino-2-hydroxybutanenitrile but suffers several mass imbalances (especially rxn_007, which is severely unbalanced with multiple missing atoms and appears chemically implausible as written). The route is structurally sound but requires significant correction of the mechanistic steps and balancing.
suggestions: Redefine the conversion from aminonitrile to amide and then to cyclic amide ensuring all atoms are accounted for.
Explicitly include water, ammonia, and potential side products as required.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This two-step direct aminonitrile-to-proline sequence is unbalanced in the final hydrolysis (rxn_009). Atom balance suggests significant loss of carbon (C-1), which could only be justified with explicit CO2 or side product formation, not given in the reaction. Chemically, no experimental evidence is cited for direct one-pot hydrolysis from this cyanohydrin all the way to proline, and mechanistically, such a multi-bond rearrangement is highly unlikely. This route needs either literature support or major correction.
suggestions: Revisit mechanistic plausibility and include intermediate amide/nitrile/amine steps.
Ensure all mass and charge conservation by explicit writing of all reactants and products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This alternative ‘thione oxidative hydrolysis’ sequence is not chemically viable as written; rxn_010 is unbalanced and misspecified (missing one carbon, two hydrogens, and an oxygen, with no plausible side products given). At least one step would have to yield another product (such as CO2, NH3, HCN, etc.) to restore mass and charge conservation. Literature does not support direct conversion of thione to proline under surface conditions. Major corrections are needed.
suggestions: Chemically verify each step in the conversion, include intermediates.

suggestions: As above, fully account for all atoms through explicit species.
Consider reactions from mechanistic precedence and checked balances.

Nitrile-amide linkages are not fully balanced (rxn_006). Mechanistically the sequence could work if all mass flows are corrected and intermediates explicitly included.
suggestions: Address mass/atom balance in all key steps as above.

However, as with P1, rxn_003 and rxn_004 are unbalanced (S and H), and rxn_011 is unbalanced in N/H. Otherwise, the pathway is chemically coherent and well-designed, but mass conservation must be satisfied in each recycling step.
suggestions: Check all network-closure steps for atom balance.
Correct S, H, N stoichiometry throughout.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is comprehensive and contains all key intermediates, reactions, and convergence points cited in the literature with alternative plausible branches. However, 7 of the 11 reactions are unbalanced per deterministic atom/charge checks, including essential steps (e.g., canonical reductive deoxygenation and thione-to-nitrile exchange). This creates major chemical feasibility issues, lowering overall confidence. Mechanistically, the canonical (Patel et al., 2015) route structure is accurate and aligns with surface cyanosulfidic chemistry. Environmental and literature consistency are excellent. The main barrier is mass conservation: each unbalanced step must be revised by explicitly including all reactants/products (as inferred, e.g., S8, H2, NH3, CO2, etc. as needed). Only then can the network be approved for prebiotic L-Proline synthesis. Otherwise, pathway coherence and target achievement are strong. Approval cannot be granted (overall_confidence < 0.9) until mass/charge conservation is strictly enforced in all reactions.
